item.title: Why We Hesitate to Contact Old Friends
item.description:
Friends

Why We Hesitate to Contact Old Friends

Rekindling old friendships has its risks and rewards.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • As we age, we often become interested in connecting with people from our past.
  • Three different motives trigger our desire to reconnect.
  • Rekindling old relationships can carry some risks; we need to proceed carefully.
Source: PeopleImages/Shutterstock

As I have gotten older, I am more interested than I used to be in people I knew a long time ago. Throughout most of my adult years, I kept my head down working hard on my career, caring for my family, and planning for the future. I had little time or interest in thinking much about the past.

As I moved into my late fifties and sixties, however, life began to slow down, and I found myself wondering about what had happened to the people I knew when I was young. As luck would have it, these years also coincided with the rise of social media, which provided a quick and convenient way to reconnect with my past life.

Most of the time, reconnection has been fun and well worth it for myself and for others who have shared their experiences with me. For example, my wife recently reconnected with her best friend from childhood, and the resurrection of their friendship is proving to be a joyful and gratifying experience for both of them.

But I have been a bit surprised at the hesitation I sometimes feel when reaching out to old friends, and others have reported this same ambivalence to me when the topic comes up in conversation.

When choosing between “letting sleeping dogs lie” and reviving old relationships, it can be useful to think about why you are reaching out.

Motives for Rekindling Old Friendships

One can have a variety of intertwined reasons for connecting with old friends:

  1. Sometimes, reconnection can be triggered by the simple desire to find out what happened to someone who was once very important to you; someone for whom you had felt genuine affection. You sincerely hope they are happy and have done well.
  2. The urge to reconnect may also be a thinly disguised way of connecting with your younger self. When we get old, we are no longer as attractive, athletic, graceful, or mentally agile as we once were. Depending upon your life circumstances, you may find yourself surrounded by people who have only known you as a middle-aged or even older person. Consequently, friends from your past may help you connect with the person you once were, for better or worse. Reminiscing with people who knew you back in the day can refresh and embellish memories of more exciting and hopeful times. These connections can be mutually energizing, at least in the short term.
  3. Psychologist Erik Erikson proposed that humans pass through a series of eight developmental stages in the course of their lifetimes. Each stage confronts the individual with a psychological crisis or conflict that must be resolved for the person to move on healthily. For older adults (over age 65 for Erikson), the person must navigate between what Erikson called integrity versus despair. During this stage, we reflect upon our lives and assess how well we have done. Do we feel a sense of accomplishment, fulfillment, wisdom, and peace, or do we feel regret and disappointment in ourselves as we wallow in the stench of despair? Do we feel like we have wasted our lives by failing to achieve anything meaningful? Have we repeatedly let other people down, be they spouses, children, friends, or parents?

Reconnecting with old schoolmates and childhood friends can help us make these judgments. After all, they are the same age as we are and they started in the same place that we did; they provide a reference point for assessing the trajectory of our own growth. By comparing our life situations, professional achievements, and happiness level to those of our old friends, we can more accurately gauge where we now stand.

These different motives for reconnecting with old friends are not mutually exclusive. In most cases, all three operate to some extent.

Are There Risks to Reconnecting with Old Friends?

There are considerations before contacting old friends. If you parted ways many years ago under bad circumstances, a reunion can be double-edged. On the one hand, it offers an opportunity for apologies and fence-mending, but reopening old wounds and reliving an ugly scene are risks, leaving both you and your former friend feeling worse than you would have if a reunion had never occurred.

Even if an old friendship faded quite naturally under good circumstances, reconnection poses risks. You and your old friends may be very different people than you once were, and issues that did not matter in your youth may now matter quite a bit. For example, many Americans have had unpleasant and uncomfortable surprises in recent years when it quickly became clear that they and a dear friend who were once quite simpatico are now on opposite sides of the political culture wars.

One should also tread lightly when reaching out to a friend known to have had hard times, especially if your own life appears, at least from the outside, to have been very happy and successful. Even if your motives are sincere and well-meaning, it may be easy for your old friend to perceive gloating or pity behind your overtures if not handled with sensitivity.

item.title: When Someone Won't See How Their Behavior Impacts Others
item.description:
Relationships

When Someone Won't See How Their Behavior Impacts Others

Trying to "explain" to someone how they're behaving can be a perilous endeavor.

Posted September 2, 2026

It’s incredibly frustrating to be in a relationship with someone unaware of how they behave in the world, how they are perceived by other people, and how their behavior actually impacts others. It's maddening and sad to watch someone who acts in ways that are aggressive, rude, dismissive, arrogant, or just off-putting, but then complains about the reactions they receive, or blames other people for their responses. It's exhausting to listen to someone who claims to always be misunderstood and misjudged; a perpetual victim who takes no responsibility or is blind to their own part in the responses they receive.

My guess, if you’re reading this article, is that you’ve already tried to communicate to this person about how they behave in the world and why people are reacting to them the way they are. My guess, too, is that by explaining or pointing out their behavior, you haven’t been able to move the dial — not because you haven’t explained it well, but usually because the person who “doesn’t know” how they’re coming across to others is someone who, at some level, has rejected how they’re being perceived, and built a whole emotional defense system to protect themselves from feeling insecure and inadequate. They are probably someone who, over time, has become unable to hear feedback about their own behavior. The two conditions frequently come together—lack of (or selective) awareness and unwillingness to consider responsibility.

But just in case you haven’t tried this most basic line of action—to simply point out to the other person how their behavior is coming across in the world and impacting other people—or even if you have tried but it hasn’t worked, here are some basics to keep in mind.

Pick the right time

Only approach the topic of their behavior when the other person is calm and in a good place, feeling secure and hopefully good about themselves. Also, only address the issue when you feel secure in the relationship, with a sense that they trust and feel connected and safe with you. Furthermore, make sure that they’re not physically or emotionally exhausted, not overwhelmed with stressors like work or health, and not distracted with too many things on their to-do list. Finally, don’t approach them when they’re about to sit down to watch the soccer game they’ve been looking forward to, or to do something they just want to fully enjoy.

It may seem like a long list of conditions to have to adhere to just to have a conversation about their behavior. And, those moments that meet all these requirements are few and far between. But timing is critical, and the reality is, if you really want to move the dial, you have to give yourself the best chance. People who are blind to their own behavior and how it impacts others are often not just defensive, but also somewhat fragile emotionally. Often, they’ve built up strong defenses to protect themselves from negative feedback, all of which you will be navigating as you try to convey your message and get through their emotional armor. That said, use the cheat sheet below, with one caveat: Don’t blame yourself if, even when adhering to all these strategies, they can’t hear you and can’t take responsibility for their own behavior. It’s not your failing. This is a complicated request for them, and more often than not, requires more than just explaining the behavior, even when the time is right.

Be specific

When you approach the unaware person, have specific examples to offer: where and how they behaved that “may” have landed differently than they imagine. When trying to point out their behavior to them, it’s important not to be vague or generalize their behavior; if they feel that you’re criticizing their character, the chances of being heard are slim (remember the fragility). Keep the focus on specific things they did or said and leave out any interpretations of their behavior or judgment calls on your part.

Again, this may feel like a thousand hoops to have to jump through, just to be heard properly, and while I wish I had a better way to address this, the reality is simply, yes, that’s true. There are a thousand hoops to jump through when dealing with someone who lacks self-awareness. Frequently, it’s an emotional minefield. They didn’t develop their level of ignorance and their disconnection between their behavior and other people’s responses without employing denial and defensiveness. Chances are, they’ve been rejecting their own accountability for a long time; it’s a piece of work to get through a system that’s protected them. It does indeed require careful planning and mindfulness.

Use I statements and integrate your insights with positive feedback

When you present someone in denial or lacking awareness with commentary on their behavior, be careful to present your case as your experience, which is supported by the responses and feedback they receive. “What I notice is that when you raise your voice with people, while you’re not meaning it to hurt, people tend to move away from you and then maybe not follow up for future contact.” Or, for example, “I know from my own experience that when people give me their writing to read, they’re putting themselves in a very vulnerable place. So, I try to remember that people are fragile and can quickly become wounded and go straight to feeling inadequate. I don’t sense that many people can be told, at least not as the first thing they hear, what’s wrong with their writing. While you have great wisdom to share, I notice that sometimes you can lead with the criticism, which can be tough for people to take in. I say that because I also notice that when you do start with what they’ve done wrong, people tend to shut down and stop listening, and then don’t follow up with you again. I’m wondering if sometimes you find that response as well?”

Point out the reality

Reality is the results that they’re actually getting from their behavior, regardless of what they think about that behavior. Point out the simple fact that what they’re doing is not producing the results they say they want (better and different responses). Keep bringing their attention to the bare bones of reality without interpretation: What they’re doing is not producing the results they want.“You often mention that you wish you had more friends. That’s true, right? And yet, however you’re interacting with other people doesn’t seem to be making that happen. In my experience, when something isn’t working, I think it can be helpful to look at what we’re doing, the part we’re playing in the situation, and maybe experiment with changing it, so we get more of what we want. One thing we know for sure is that if we keep doing the same thing, we’ll keep getting the same result.” This is just a purely results-based argument, which can deactivate their defensiveness.

These are basic communication strategies you can try, all of which you’ve probably already tried. In part three, I’ll offer a Plan B for a path forward after the words have failed. Stay tuned.

item.title: You Don’t Have to Wait for Life to Calm Down
item.description:
Motivation

You Don’t Have to Wait for Life to Calm Down

A new study suggests external pressure steals your peace but not your purpose.

Posted September 2, 2026

What if the assumptions we make about meaning, motivation and pressure are not quite as true as we think?
Source: Mika Baumeister / Unsplash

Most people have a version of this thought (I know I do): I’ll start living for what matters once things ease up. Once the pressure lifts and the schedule lightens. Once the tedious obligations quieten down. Once there is finally some room to breathe. Then meaning becomes possible again. We think this as if stress takes up so much space that there is none left for purpose.

A new study questions that assumption.

The study, published in the International Journal of Applied Positive Psychology, set out to understand what drives the sense that life is meaningful (Le Guellaff Pallin, 2026). Using data from 429 participants and three statistical approaches, the researchers compared two possibilities. One was that meaning depends on the balance between autonomous motivation, wanting what you pursue, and controlled motivation, which is driven by pressure, guilt or obligation. The other was that autonomous motivation matters more directly, regardless of how much pressure is also present.

The balance model lost.

What Pressure Does to Meaning

External pressure was associated with distress in the study, but it was not directly associated with lower meaning. Controlled motivation—the feeling of being pushed by obligation, guilt or external demands—was consistently associated with distress. Anxiety and depressive symptoms were higher among participants who reported being more strongly driven by pressure rather than genuine want.

Controlled motivation did not have a direct effect on meaning, however, once autonomous motivation was taken into account.

The two forces appear to operate on separate tracks: Pressure showed up in distress, while autonomous motivation showed up in meaning. Someone can feel strongly autonomous about a goal and highly pressured at the same time. The pressure does not necessarily cancel out the wanting.

I found that reassuring.

The Caveat

This matters most for the people who keep waiting: If you believe external pressure directly blocks meaning, the logical thing to do is reduce the pressure first. Wait until life opens up and deal with the obligations and then, when everything is finally under control, ask yourself what matters to you.

Life does not always cooperate with that plan.

If pressure and meaningful direction can operate separately, waiting for the pressure to disappear before asking what matters to you may be unnecessary. The pressure may not be reducible right now. You can still ask what you want, what you really care about and whether your life is moving in that direction.

The authors make a similar point: Meaning may not need to wait for pressure to subside. Eliminating external demands may not be the only route. Identifying what you enjoy, and finding ways to move towards it while those demands remain, may matter too.

Motivation May Predict Anxiety and Depressive Symptoms

The study found that controlled motivation was associated with anxiety and depressive symptoms, but it would be a mistake to read these findings as an argument for simply putting up with an unhealthy level of pressure.

What the findings suggest instead is that pressure and meaning may not be opposites. Pressure can affect your wellbeing, your sleep and how distressed you feel without necessarily erasing your sense that what you are doing matters.

You might be exhausted and still find meaning in the work. You might be under real pressure while moving towards something you want. You might even experience both at the same time.

item.title: What Drives a Killer Instinct for Success
item.description:
Motivation

What Drives a Killer Instinct for Success

How we hold onto persistence, resilience, and commitment when motivation fades.

Posted September 2, 2026

We often describe highly successful people as having something others lack: ambition, discipline, hunger, or what is sometimes called a “killer instinct.” They seem able to tolerate rejection, pursue difficult goals for years, and continue working long after the initial excitement may have disappeared. This can make success look like a personality lottery, as though some people are naturally equipped to win, while others are not.

Psychological research suggests something more complicated. Achievement is rarely about intelligence or talent alone but how people regulate behaviour, interpret failure, tolerate discomfort, delay gratification, and remain committed when rewards are distant.

One of the central difficulties of goal pursuit is that the cost is immediate while the reward is delayed. Research on delay discounting shows that people tend to value immediate rewards more strongly than delayed ones, even when the delayed outcome is objectively more valuable (Frederick, Loewenstein, & O'Donoghue, 2002). People who achieve difficult goals, then, may be unusually capable of allowing a distant future to influence present behaviour.

This is closely connected to self-regulation. Carver and Scheier (1998) proposed that people regulate behaviour partly by comparing their current position with a desired state. Yet the same gap can produce very different reactions. One person thinks, “I am not there yet, so I need to keep working.” Another thinks, “I am not there yet, so perhaps I am not capable.”

Beliefs about ability matter here. Dweck's (2006) work on mindset suggests that people who see ability as developable are more likely to treat difficulty as something that can be worked through rather than as evidence of inadequacy. A rejected application can mean, “I need another strategy” or “I am not good enough.” The first interpretation keeps behaviour moving. The second can terminate it.

This may explain why successful people often appear unusually resilient. They're not immune to rejection but perhaps less likely to turn every negative outcome into a judgement about who they are.

Duckworth and colleagues (2007) described grit as perseverance and passion for long-term goals. Although later research questioned how much grit predicts beyond traits such as conscientiousness, perseverance itself remains important (Credé, Tynan, & Harms, 2017). Almost anyone can work hard while a goal feels exciting. The more revealing effort comes later, after the fifth application, the 20th rejection, the third revision, or the ninth month of nobody noticing the effort.

This is where motivation and commitment separate. Motivation is an emotional state, and emotional states fluctuate. Commitment can survive those fluctuations. Highly driven people may not wake up motivated every morning. They may simply have learned not to make action dependent on motivation.

Bandura (1997) defined self-efficacy as the belief that one can organise and execute the actions needed to achieve an outcome. Importantly, self-efficacy develops through mastery experiences. Surviving difficulty teaches the individual that future difficulty may also be survivable. The person who has recovered from rejection may experience the next rejection differently. It still hurts, but it no longer predicts ultimate failure.

What we call a “killer instinct” may partly be a high tolerance for psychological discomfort. Difficult goals expose people to boredom, uncertainty, criticism, comparison, embarrassment, frustration, and fear of failure. Some interpret these emotions as signals to stop. Others learn that discomfort and action can coexist. Research on psychological flexibility suggests that adaptive functioning involves continuing to behave in accordance with meaningful values even while experiencing difficult thoughts and emotions (Kashdan & Rottenberg, 2010).

Identity may provide the final piece. Identity-based motivation theory suggests that people are more likely to act in ways that feel consistent with who they believe they are (Oyserman, 2009). There is a psychological difference between saying “I want to write” and “I am a writer.” Once a goal becomes part of one's identity, action becomes less dependent on daily negotiation.

Perhaps this is the real meaning of the so-called killer instinct—not ruthlessness but an ability to tolerate delayed rewards, recover from setbacks, remain active while uncomfortable, and distinguish temporary failure from personal inadequacy.

The person who succeeds may not desire their goal more intensely than everyone else but they may have learned how to keep moving when motivation fades, progress is invisible, and the present offers little evidence that their effort will pay off. For some, this persistence is driven by something psychologically stronger: the fear of losing what they have already invested or having to live with the possibility that they gave up too soon. Those with the “killer instinct” may keep moving because, psychologically, the pain of surrender feels greater than the comfort of stopping.

item.title: Can a Stepparent Buy Love?
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Can a Stepparent Buy Love?

How tangible support can shape stepchild-stepparent relationships.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • A stepparent's financial support can help make relationships with stepchildren better.
  • Financial support does not have to be large to be important to stepchildren.
  • Helping children pay for things that matter to them builds bonds.
  • It helps stepparents when someone else points out to stepchildren the financial support they receive.

Can money buy a stepparent love from a stepchild? Well, the Beatles (and other songwriters) have told us, “No. Money can’t buy you love." But research tells us, “Maybe,” or “It depends,” or “Sometimes.” Let me explain.

Researchers studying stepparents and minor-aged stepchildren have reported that a stepparent’s generosity can contribute to more positive relationships with stepchildren. In a review of research that my colleagues and I wrote, we clunkily called this dynamic "stepparents providing stepchildren with tangible goods and resources," which is an academic way of talking about stepparents giving stepchildren “stuff.”

The “stuff” that stepparents give to their stepchildren that benefits their relationships ranges widely, from buying stepchildren ice cream, candy, and other small treats to paying for college tuition, purchasing a car for a stepchild, or just generally raising the stepchild’s standard of living. By standard of living, we mean things like providing bigger houses or apartments in nicer neighborhoods, purchasing name-brand clothing instead of discount brands, going on vacations, and being able to stream more entertainment services than before the stepparent arrived on the scene.

Supporting stepchildren with tangible “stuff” may sound expensive, but it does not have to be. For example, we interviewed a stepfather who told us that bonding with his stepchildren seemed to change for the better after he spontaneously bought them ice cream cones when they were running errands one day. In a separate interview, this man’s 12-year-old stepson told us that a turning point in their relationship was when his stepdad asked them if he wanted ice cream before they went home from running errands. This small act of generosity struck the stepson as a significant and memorable event because his parents had never been able to afford extra treats like ice cream cones. This boy, struck by his stepfather’s kind gesture, told us he thought, “This guy is ok. He must really like us to buy ice cream! I hope he and my mom stay together, because I could get used to this.”

Another stepson remembered when his stepfather was getting to know him that they bonded over their love for the St. Louis Cardinals. The clincher in becoming closer was his stepfather taking him to some Cardinals’ games and buying him a baseball glove he had wanted for a long time. The young man recalled it this way: “He took me to games, bought me baseball equipment for my little league games, and generally bought me things to get me to like him.” Grinning, he went on, “And it worked.” Buying stuff for stepchildren also works for stepmothers, of course.

Earlier, I said that buying stuff works to enhance stepparent-stepchild bonding only sometimes, and that it may depend on various factors. First, to provide tangible support to facilitate bonding, a stepchild must notice that the stepparent is buying them things or paying for new experiences. In other words, stepchildren must be aware of a stepparent’s generosity for it to matter to them. Second, the meanings that stepchildren attach to a stepparent’s financial support need to be positive for the relationship to benefit. Research does not provide many clues about how to make this happen, other than it seems logical that stepchildren are more likely to frame financial support in positive ways when the support allows them to do things that are important to them (for example, paying for a school they want to attend, paying for music lessons they want), and when stepparents are genuine in helping their stepchildren financially.

It also likely helps when someone else, such as a parent or an older sibling, points out to stepchildren that their stepparent is paying for stuff because he or she wants to help, and not because they are legally obligated to do so. Finally, it seems logical that being consistent in financially supporting stepchildren over time may help them appreciate a stepparent’s help — as opposed to inconsistently offering financial support or using money as a “carrot” to bribe the child to engage in certain desired behaviors.

So, money can’t be counted on to “buy” a stepchild’s love, but then again, it can’t hurt. In fact, research indicates that financially supporting stepchildren, along with getting to know them better (see "First Steps for Stepparents"), becoming their friend or mentor (see "Having Fun with Stepchildren"), working with stepchildren on projects (see "Getting Closer to Stepchildren Through Working Together"), being an ally when they have disagreements with other people (see "Becoming an Ally to Stepchildren"), are all ways to build closer ties to stepchildren.

item.title: Good Thoughts, Bad Thoughts
item.description:
Authenticity

Good Thoughts, Bad Thoughts

On intrusive thoughts and your agency.

Posted September 2, 2026

I met with a client for a few weeks. She always felt somewhere else, as if there were always something more important for her to listen to. But this distraction held nothing blissful or light in it; it was full of tension and nervousness instead. It was as if she were being pulled off into far distances without her permission, and every time she had to start from scratch to recover her focus.

For weeks this part of her behavior only slightly bothered me, but I took it as my own bias and moved on—as a teacher, I am constantly dealing with easily distractible people. It was when I realized that she was the first to be bothered by it that I decided to intervene.

She was trying to complete her own thoughts and describe the feelings gathering around that experience, but it was like a dance. She would start talking, then get lost without words, then move again toward a new fragment of the same speech. When I asked her if there was anything bothering her, she said: "There are a lot of thoughts today."

She said it the way you'd remark on the weather. An observation about the state of things.

"A lot of thoughts about what?" I asked.

She smiled and didn't know how to explain. Then she looked at the wall, as if to gather focus. "I don't know yet. I'm still looking at them. They're not all for me. Better to choose a few, or the space runs out."

I have sat with that sentence for a long time. I'm still looking at them—not I have them, not they're mine. She was watching her thoughts the way you'd watch something pass by the window—the leaves, a plastic bag lifted by the wind, both at once. In my years of practice I have almost never heard anyone speak of thought this way. Most of us possess our thoughts. We defend them, negotiate with them, identify with them so completely that we can no longer tell where we end and the thought begins.

She had not yet decided which thoughts were hers.

Intrusive Thoughts: The Traffic We Don't Direct

We like to imagine the mind as a room we own, into which we invite the thoughts we choose. The truth is closer to what my client described: The room is already full when she walks in, with cruel flashes about someone she loves, catastrophic images that arrive uninvited—leaving her child at school, then instantly picturing her daughter in distress after a small accident with huge repercussions. She knew, rationally, that leaving her child at school does not summon catastrophe. And yet, and yet.

This is the ordinary condition, not the pathological one. Intrusive thoughts—the violent image, the shameful impulse, the sudden what if I—are nearly universal. Research on the phenomenon has found that the overwhelming majority of people experience unwanted, intrusive thoughts they would never act on and do not endorse. What varies is how much we believe they are us.

My client's suffering was that she believed the space was scarce and that every thought entering it made some claim on her. She had no filter yet. That wasn't a defect; no one had yet taught her that a filter is not a wall. The thoughts enter regardless of our efforts; we must decide when to take ownership of them and to understand that we are not each of them.

What the Stoics Knew About the Door

Long before we had a clinical language for intrusive thoughts, the Stoics had mapped this exact terrain. Epictetus taught that we are disturbed not by things but by our judgments about things—and, crucially, that the first impression, the phantasia that strikes the mind unbidden, is not yet in our power. What is in our power is assent—whether we take up that impression, endorse it, let it become a settled belief about ourselves and the world.

A thought arrives. That much is not chosen; the wind brings it. What we choose is whether to say yes to it; whether to hand it the keys. Marcus Aurelius returned to this discipline again and again in his notebooks, reminding himself that the mind takes the color of its thoughts only when it dyes itself in them repeatedly. A thought passed through is weather. A thought assented to, day after day, sensation after sensation, becomes a groove — and eventually a self.

This is what my client intuited without the vocabulary. "The thoughts aren't ours," she said once, when she thought I was not listening. "We identify with some of them. There's a world of thoughts around us and we decide which to take, which to work on more often, which to speak—until we become some of those thoughts."

She had arrived at the Stoic discipline of assent. What she had not yet been given was permission to use it gently.

The Grooves We Choose

Here is where the Stoic frame meets something the ancients said less about: self-compassion. The discipline of assent can curdle into another kind of tyranny—a policing of every thought, a vigilance that treats each intrusive image as a moral test to be passed. We feel guilty, inappropriate, or ashamed for having certain thoughts; on the other hand, we feel proud when good thoughts cross our mind. Neither of those cases equates to freedom. That is the same exhaustion in a philosopher's robe.

My client seems to have spent years as a kind of radio receiving every frequency at once, straining to make out which one was hers. Her migraines came, I think, from the sheer labor of it — the belief that she had to hold every thought, honor every one, or betray something. What finally reached her was someone sitting beside her, putting a hand between her shoulders, and telling her, You don't become every person who walks across the room. So you don't have to become every thought, either.

That is the missing half of the Stoic teaching. Yes, we choose which impressions we assent to. But we choose them the way a gardener chooses, not the way a judge condemns. The thoughts we let pass are not enemies defeated; they are simply guests we did not seat. The grooves that thoughts carve in us—Marcus's dyed mind—form through repetition, through the sensations we return to again and again. Which means that we have real agency, but it is slow and kind. We do shape our inner life patiently, by what we keep choosing to attend to.

To Let the Thought Go By

There was nothing in particular devouring my client from within. There was only a person who had maybe learned too well to receive the whole voice of the world, and had not yet learned that she was allowed to choose her own.

Some of us are crossed by more, some by fewer; none of us chose the traffic. Our vitality is in the self-compassion we owe ourselves: to not take ownership of every thought that passes through, to choose the few that will become ours, and to watch the rest go by the window, the way you'd watch the leaves, or a plastic bag lifted by the wind, both at once.
